# Economic Focus **Europe’s Atlas** The significance of the German economy in Europe is starkly apparent. Europe’s largest economy accounts for approximately 30% of total output of the Eurozone. Through the first half of this year the strength of the German economy prevented a Eurozone-wide recession. Growth has been driven by export demand and robust domestic consumption. However, storm clouds are on the horizon as demand for German exports appears to be weakening. Producing the goods for export, the manufacturing sector is at risk from a slowdown in external demand. ## **GDP and Manufacturing Output (Index Jan 2008 = 100) Exports and new export orders** 60 20%

**Producing the goods** Manufacturing output suffered a peak-to-trough contraction of 21.4% (between Q1 2008 and Q1 2009), much more severe than GDP which contracted 6.8% (see chart on left above). As the manufacturing sector roared back into life in the second half of 2009 so too did the economy. Germany was the first developed economy in Europe to recover to pre-crisis levels of economic output, doing so back in Q2 2011. Given that most major economies in Europe are suffering from acutely depressed industrial sectors, and probably a permanent loss of capacity, Germany stands out as an exception. Germany’s swift bounce back was aided by a weaker euro boosting export demand. But, competitive product markets and availability of spare capacity in the manufacturing sector were also key to the revival. Germany is producing goods that emerging economies are demanding. **Storm clouds gather** Export growth has generally been slowing despite driving the Germany economy in H1, due to weak demand in Europe and cooling in emerging economies. Furthermore, the outlook is bleak as export orders contract. The PMI index for new export orders fell to 39.5 in August – the further below 50 the stronger the contractionary Economic Focus sentiment among manufacturing managers (see chart on right above). This is a concern for the domestic industries that manufacture goods for export. ## **Manufacturing output index and capacity utilisation (%) Investment in machinery and equipment (€ Bn 2005)** 105 95 40

**Rise of the machines** Germany enjoyed a rise in manufacturing output from the mid-1990s, virtually uninterrupted until the Great Recession. Manufacturing output grew by 44% between 1995 and 2008 (see chart above). With capacity utilisation largely flat over this period (around 85-90%), it is implied that output growth has been facilitated by expanding manufacturing capacity. Capacity expansion is delivered by investing in machinery and equipment and investment in this area rose by to 42% over 2003-2008. While manufacturing output is close to the pre-crisis levels, investment is languishing 9% below peak levels. Output cannot outpace investment indefinitely. Is there a looming capacity crunch? **Weak demand or lack of capacity?** Undoubtedly export demand is weak, which is a concern for the manufacturing base. But, capacity could also become an issue. Although capacity utilization is currently around 85%, suggesting a little slack, it is worth noting that utilization rarely exceeds this level by much even when demand is strong. We suggest that weakening demand for German exports might be disguising an issue of tight capacity in the manufacturing sector. Lower than expected investment in machinery and equipment fuels this inclination. The chart below shows the value of large, new business loans (greater than €1 million and longer than 5 years), potentially the type of loans used for capacity expansions. Through the first half of 2012 this type of loan was in decline. ## **New business loans (€ billion)** 9

Are manufacturers being cautious, reluctant to invest in new capacity at levels seen prior to the crisis? Exercising caution when the global outlook is plagued with uncertainties and confidence is low makes sense. Or is there an alternative reason why investment is subdued? Could manufacturers be having difficulty in securing loans for capital investment projects because of tight credit? European banks are having to recapitalize and shrinking loan books is one way to achieve this. We cannot be certain which is true but in some respects the cause of lower investment is not important. What does matter is that the recovery in investment in machinery and equipment has not kept pace with that of output. If underinvestment results in tight capacity in one of Europe’s biggest growth drivers, German exports may be constrained when demand picks up again.
